newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian firms say industry not competitive.
newsitem.headline: Austrian firms say industry not competitive.

text.p: Austrian firms have few regrets about joining the European Union, but warn that industry must become more competitive if it is going to survive in the tough new market of Europe.
Speaking ahead of European parliamentary elections on October 13, key industrial figures said Austria had to advance on the political and economic front.

"Austrian firms basically have a good chance of doing well in the European Union, but we must adjust to being in a big market," Otto Wolfrum, member of the board of food retailer Mautner Markhof, said on Monday.
"Altogether Austrian workers must be more mobile, learn languages and be prepared to move abroad, then Austria will be successful," he added.

"European competition is getting tougher all the time, which means we permanently have to increase productivity and lower personnel costs," said Randolf Fochler, spokesman for high-grade steel maker Boehler-Uddeholm.
Wolfrum blamed a weak competitive streak in industry on the political system in Austria, which has Europe's largest welfare programme under a Social Democrat-led coalition government.
"Austria has the highest wage costs in Europe -- too many holidays, too many public holidays, and 13th and 14th month payments," he noted. "That must change."
Austrian employees receive two additional month's payments as extra holiday and Christmas remunerations.
Austria's membership of the EU from January 1995 has not had a major impact on its large, export-oriented companies which already had a strong foothold in Europe.
But some firms in smaller sectors like the food industry have felt the pinch from more competition and price pressure.

While seeking improvements in Austria's industrial and political structures, leading industrialists warned not to rush into Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU), scheduled to begin in 1999.
"On the whole we are positive about EMU, but we may be going too fast for Austria with the Euro (the EU's proposed single currency)," said Boehler's Fochler.

VA Technologie's chief executive Othmar Puehringer said Austria's hard currency, the schilling, had forced industry to become more competitive. The schilling has been tied to the German mark for more than two decades.
But Dionys Lehner of textile firm Linz Textil warned that Italy and even Germany were not well-enough prepared for EMU.
"Short-term measures are not sufficient, the infrastructure must be changed," he said. Linz Textil saw 75 percent of its market destroyed by the collapse of the Italian lira three years ago.
